newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton hails Australia's racial melting pot.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails Australia's racial melting pot.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, taking issue with anti-immigrant sentiment in the United States and Australia, argued on Thursday that ethnic diversity was a source of strength and a cause for pride.

Speaking at a harbourside park with the soaring Sydney Opera House in the background, a tired, hoarse-sounding Clinton said Sydney's 2000 Summer Olympics would showcase the melting pot heritage that Australians and Americans share.

In a speech billed as an address to the Australian people, Clinton urged them to think about how every day they accepted people whose roots were in Britain, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East or Africa.

"Every day that you do that when the world is looking at you, you offer a rebuke to those who would take away the lives and futures and the fortunes of the children of this world because they are different," Clinton said.
In a country that has given the U.S. president a very warm welcome, Clinton's speech got a peculiarly mute reception from a crowd of a few thousand people.

Race and immigration has become the subject of a very sensitive national debate in Australia since a maverick politician, Pauline Hanson, complained in parliament in September that Australia was being swamped by Asians.
Clinton said the greatest challenge facing the world in the next century was to find a way "to let our children define themselves in terms of who they are, not who they are not".

"I cannot think of a better place in the entire world, a more shining example of how people can come together as one nation and one community than Sydney, Australia. I'm so grateful that you'll be here for the Olympics in 2000," he said.

Clinton's speech to the people of Australia was his only public event on a day otherwise devoted to jogging, sightseeing and the fulfilment of a duffer's dream -- a round of golf with Australian golf idol Greg Norman.

Clinton, in the midst of a five-day working holiday "Down Under," said he needed a break after the rigours of his recent re-election campaign and told reporters he was enjoying himself, saying: "It's great!"
He is in the Asian-Pacific region for meetings in Manila with leaders of China, Japan and South Korea on Sunday and the one-day Asia-Pacific Ecomomic Cooperation summit the next day

After jogging in the Royal Botanic Gardens in the centre of Sydney on Thursday morning, the president made an impromptu stop at the landmark opera house and got a surprised security guard to give him a tour.

He said he was especially interested in the Sydney Opera House having played the saxophone as a youth. "This is one of the most famous buildings in the world. I didn't want to come all the way to Sydney and not see it," he said.
Later, Clinton and his wife Hillary went shopping, and the president purchased a broad-brimmed Australian bush hat, saying he had one like it but it was "just about worn out".

Clinton's golf game with Norman had some potential for embarrassment, etiquette-wise as well as athletic. During his re-election campaign, when he was riding high in the polls over Republican rival Bob Dole, Clinton regularly warned complacent aides: "Remember Greg Norman".

That was a reference to the fact that the world's greatest golfer went into the final round of April's U.S. Masters with a six-stroke lead only to lose by five strokes to Britain's Nick Faldo, burnishing his reputation as a "choker."
After the golf game, the Clintons were flying to Australia's tropical north for two days at the Great Barrier Reef resort town of Port Douglas. They will leave on Saturday for the Philippines.
